churrasco.title: Churrasco: the culinary fire of Brazil

blocks.text:
**Churrasco** – the word alone sounds like flaming embers and hissing fire. And the name probably comes from the very sound that dripping fat makes as it burns. In Brazil, on the Iberian Peninsula (Portugal and Spain) and in parts of Latin America, Churrasco thus aptly describes a way of preparing meat that poetically carries its special features in its name.

In terms of taste, Churrasco stands for intensity, passion and, not least, authenticity. Our Churrasco steakhouse takes as its model the so-called gauchos, European immigrants to Brazil in the 19th century. They gathered around large fires, over which they grilled their meat skewers together in convivial company. In our restaurant, we want to offer our guests this convivial atmosphere while serving them the best meat skewers they have ever tasted.
What is Churrasco?

The **Churrasco** method combines traditional grilling skills with modern culinary finesse. At our Churrascaria in Zurich, we offer Churrasco Rodizio. In broad terms, Churrasco grilling works like this:

items:
The meat is cut into hand-sized pieces. Popular meats for Churrasco are beef, chicken, lamb and pork, as well as various kinds of sausage. Among the most popular Churrasco dishes are beef tenderloin and chicken leg.
→ In Brazilian Churrasco, which we offer in our restaurant, the most popular dishes are Picanha (rump cap, “Tafelspitz”) and Coxa de frango (chicken thigh).
About half an hour before grilling, the pieces of meat are sprinkled by hand with coarse salt and/or given a hearty marinade.
The pieces of meat are then threaded onto large skewers.
The meat is grilled fat side down first – either over charcoal or over an open fire. After that, in Churrasco Rodizio, the skewers are turned continuously.

Before serving, it is customary with larger steaks to cut the meat again down the middle or into several smaller, bite-sized pieces. With our Churrasco Rodizio, we bring the meat straight to the tables and carve it into small slices there.

Churrasco is a group experience, so it is traditionally served on a large platter from which all the guests help themselves. In our Churrascaria, the skewers are served to each individual guest right at the table.
It is customary to serve side dishes such as salads, garlic bread, polenta and potato salad.

blocks.text: Depending on the region, there are certain differences in the types of meat, the way the meat is prepared, the ingredients and the way it is served.
Regional variations of Churrasco

In Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, **Churrasco** is known mainly as a beef steak, served with salad and chips or mashed potatoes. In Brazil, on the other hand, any meat grilled on a churrasqueira (the special Churrasco grill) is called Churrasco. So-called Churrascaria restaurants are widespread in Brazil, affordable for the general population and often the hub of social life. In many parts of the world, Churrasco restaurants take the Brazilian concept as their model – and so does Boinabrasa!
An exciting and fun way to barbecue

Compared with the charcoal grill so widespread in Europe, Churrasco grilling makes the meat considerably crispier and gives it a hearty, fiery aroma. Gourmets appreciate the charred note the meat takes on, as well as the look of the dark reddish-brown crust. It calls for a firm bite, but the flavour literally explodes as your teeth sink in. By then at the latest, you realise that while the meat is very crispy on the outside, it is deliciously juicy on the inside!

Churrasco is not only fun to eat but also to prepare. The grill master can practically feel himself playing with the fire and preparing the meat the way our ancestors did at great feasts. Of course, care must be taken and a suitable distance kept! Anyone who has never eaten Churrasco should first dine at a Churrascaria before trying it at home.
Visit us at our Churrascaria in Zurich!

If you want to experience authentic Churrasco with your family, friends or colleagues, we warmly invite you to our Churrasco restaurant – in other words, to our Churrascaria in Zurich! Our steakhouse not only prepares meat the Brazilian way; we also bring the culture of the Brazilian gauchos together in our ambience, our staff uniforms and our cheerful team. The Churrasco skewers are our stars, but our desserts and drinks also have a South American touch. Ever tried Brazilian beer? It tastes excellent! Our buffets give you the chance to try just about everything – which is why they are so popular.

Curious? Why not reserve your table at our Churrascaria today, bring along a few of your favourite people and look forward to a steakhouse of a very special, culinary-exotic kind. We look forward to your visit!

blocks.text: You too can enjoy a very special experience at our Churrascaria.

Restaurant Boinabrasa was founded in 2013 by us – a Brazilian-Swiss family – and is still run with passion and success today. With 140 indoor and 40 terrace seats, our Churrasco **steakhouse in Zurich** (Dielsdorf) has ideal capacity for all kinds of events, and several free parking spaces for our guests.
A steak restaurant with a difference
Experience Churrasco

The strength and values of our restaurant lie in the authentic, traditional preparation of “Churrasco”. Churrasco is a Brazilian grilling tradition in which juicy cuts of beef, lamb and pork as well as chicken fillet are threaded onto large skewers and grilled. This particular culinary tradition began in the early 19th century, when the gauchos (European immigrants who settled in the Rio Grande do Sul region) would gather, light a fire, skewer large pieces of meat and grill them slowly.

The exclamation “Boi na brasa!” means something like “The bull is over the embers!” – an announcement that embodies the anticipation of a delicious warm treat in a convivial atmosphere.

As a **Churrasco steakhouse** & bar, we would love to share this cheerful anticipation and conviviality with you! In this spirit, we offer you far more than steaks: we present incomparably delicious South American delights for the palate.
Rodizio steak à discrétion: a culinary trip from Zurich to Brazil

At our Churrascaria, our Churrasco grill masters – the “Churrasqueiros” – prepare juicy steak meat to an old gaucho recipe and grill it evenly on rotating skewers. Our friendly “Passadores” then bring the meat to your table, again and again, round after round, until you are completely satisfied. The Brazilian gaucho steaks are carved from the skewer individually for your plate. This traditional way of serving meat is called “Rodizio”, which literally means “that which turns”. With a kind of traffic-light system at the table (green & red button), our guests can signal to our service staff when they would like to be served meat and when not.

Our kitchen prepares only meat of the highest quality from trusted business partners:

We are already looking forward to delighting you with our delicious treats!

There is plenty of expert debate, and even philosophising, about which “cut” of beef is actually the best. Argentinians swear by entrecôte, among others; Germans and Americans increasingly go for the T-bone; and the French can never get enough of their fillet. Brazilians, however, find the part just below the tail particularly delicious: **Picanha** – also called Tafelspitz or Schwanzstück in German – is the “rump cap”, still part of the round or rump, and is known above all for its intense flavour, because Picanha tastes of beef like no other part of the animal. This is mainly because the so-called fat cap is not removed when it is cut.

Today, Picanha is traditionally one of the highlights of many South American grill parties and BBQs. With the Picanha skewer, the grill masters of the Boinabrasa Churrascaria bring this South American highlight to Swiss plates.
Picanha is a highlight of the Brazilian art of grilling

Brazilians find the Picanha cut so tasty that they import it from Argentina in huge quantities – after all, each animal yields only two of these cuts. That makes it all the more important to prepare this steak perfectly – with Churrasco, of course: the fiery, crispy method of preparation that goes back to the “gauchos” (immigrants to South America) and is still celebrated today in many Churrascarias in Brazil. Our steakhouse, modelled on “Brasileiro” Churrasco, is proud to offer this special cut as a meat skewer. And our guests just can’t get enough of it.
What makes the Picanha cut so popular

One thing can rightly be said: Brazilians know a great deal about preparing a fine steak perfectly. And when they have the choice of which cut of beef to grill, they often choose Picanha. Let’s gather the facts:

items: A **Picanha** usually weighs approx. 1.2 kg and is relatively thick. Perfect for grilling on a skewer over an open fire – in other words, Churrasco!

The fat cap, which is also relatively thick, has two functions in Churrasco: on the one hand, it protects the meat during grilling and keeps it juicy and tender. On the other, fat from it sweats into the steak and creates the characteristically intense beef flavour.
The grill master does not need to season a Picanha much: the steak is simply salted (by “massaging” the salt in), and only seconds before it goes over the flame.
This fairly simple method is easy to recreate on your own grill at home. That makes Picanha a good way into the culinary world of Churrasco.

blocks.text: All that aside: flavour always wins. One bite of a piece of Picanha is usually enough to be convinced. That explosion of beef essence on the tongue; that crisp, crunchy give as your teeth sink into juicy, tender meat. Then it has happened, and you understand why Brazilians have such a special relationship with this cut of beef.
Is “Picanha” the same as “Tafelspitz”?

When people in German-speaking countries talk about “Tafelspitz”, they usually mean a cut without the fat cap. That is an important difference! Because the fat cap is essential for the juiciness of Picanha cooked the “Brasileiro” Churrasco way. You don’t have to eat it; it is enough for the layer of fat to baste the meat during the Rodizio (the “turning on the skewer”). Sometimes a little fat drips down and burns; then it sizzles beautifully – a sound that probably once gave Churrasco its name!

In the German-speaking world, Tafelspitz is used for roulade dishes, for example, which is why the fat cap, seen as a nuisance there, is removed from the cut. Every time that happens, a Churrasqueiro somewhere in Brazil slaps his forehead – guaranteed!
Tasting Picanha together at a Churrasco Rodizio restaurant

Churrasco is, quite simply, a group experience. Bring your family, colleagues and friends to Boinabrasa, make yourselves at home in our cosy, South American-inspired atmosphere and let our Churrasqueiros – the grill masters – and our Passadores – the waiters and carvers – spoil you round after round. Alongside the recommended **Picanha** skewers, we offer **Churrasco**-style meat skewers of beef, chicken, lamb and pork. For desserts and drinks, too, we have delicious South American options – such as the original Caipirinha from Brazil. Also discover popular Brazilian desserts such as grilled pineapple or mango mousse. Everything is set for your Brazilian barbecue evening – we look forward to your visit!

Do you remember the days when chops, sausages and pork belly were mostly what ended up on the grill? And when the mention of meat on a spit made almost everyone think of classic suckling pig? Fortunately, the triumph of grilling in this part of the world, and above all traditional Brazilian “Churrasco”, has greatly expanded the menu of delicacies – and brought entirely new flavours and culinary experiences into our lives.

A delicious speciality in this context is **Maminha** and **Maminha Churrasco**. Maminha is a cut of beef that consists mainly of muscle but is heavily marbled, meaning it contains a lot of fat between the layers of muscle. This fat makes Maminha particularly flavourful, juicy and tender. The striking shape of the cut has earned Maminha many names and makes it unmistakable. Because of its triangular shape, for instance, the meat is called “Frauenschuh” (“lady’s shoe”) in some regions – it is reminiscent of a shoe that tapers to a point at the front. As it comes from the rump of the animal, it is also known as “Hüftspitze” (“rump tip”). In southern Germany and Austria it is also called “Hüferschwanzel” or “Hieferschwanzel”. And because of its particularly high quality, in some places Maminha goes by the name “Bürgermeisterstück” (“mayor’s cut”) or “Pfaffenstück” (“parson’s cut”).
Churrasco & Maminha: a unique combination

To recall once more the days when grilling was not yet as popular and varied as it is today: Maminha used to be prepared mainly as a pot roast. That is certainly a delicacy too, but we believe it does not fully do justice to Maminha’s potential. Only as a meat skewer – as **“Churrasco”** – can this cut really show off its qualities. In our Churrascaria we do not cut up the **Maminha**; we grill it whole. Only once it is cooked do we carve the meat into thick or thin slices – whichever our guests prefer. This has the advantage that the fat can release its unique aroma during grilling. On the one hand, the fat keeps the meat fibres juicy. On the other, fat is an important carrier of flavour, a natural flavour enhancer. When the fat renders during grilling or drips as liquid onto the meat and the charcoal, flavour and aroma come together in a unique composition. It makes Maminha an absolute delicacy!

So if you have always thought of pot roast as a delicacy – which, of course, it is – you really must try Maminha prepared this way. We promise a culinary “aha moment”!
Maminha vs. Picanha: which tastes better?

On the question “Maminha vs. Picanha – which offers more enjoyment?”, opinions differ. Many people find the taste of **Maminha and Picanha** similar. The differences in flavour certainly become clearest when you can try both side by side – as you naturally can at our steakhouse. Anyone comparing the tenderness of the meat will find that both Picanha and Maminha are very tender, with Picanha perhaps a touch more “buttery”. Maminha, on the other hand, is often perceived as somewhat “meatier”, i.e. our guests describe the meaty flavour of Maminha Churrasco as more pronounced. The obvious difference between Maminha and Picanha is the proportion of fat in the beef. So if lean meat matters a lot to you, you should choose Picanha.

→ Maminha is the juiciest part of the meat in the rump area. But the meat is not quite as tender as Picanha. In Brazil, Picanha is predominantly regarded as the finest cut of beef. Of course, both cuts are eaten with great enthusiasm à la Churrasco.
Enjoy the Brazilian way of life & cuisine

Come to our restaurant for **Churrasco with Maminha**, Picanha and many other meat skewers – we look forward to seeing you! You will find authentic Brazilian dishes and food here: alongside our specialities from the grill, we of course also offer other delicacies, desserts and drinks that will whisk you away to Brazil’s zest for life and its pleasures!

linguica.title: Linguiça Churrasco — the Brazilian sausage speciality grilled on the skewer

blocks.text: Linguiça is a smoked, cured sausage made from pork. The sausage speciality **Linguiça** originally comes from Portugal and is related to the paprika sausage Chouriço. Portuguese immigrants brought the recipe for what is today a typically Brazilian sausage with them to the country. Brazil was discovered in 1500 by the Portuguese explorer Pedro Alvares Cabral and was a Portuguese colony until its independence in 1822. That is how Portuguese became established as the national language and how many goods, wares and foods from Portugal found their way to the largest country in South America.
The ingredients of the Brazilian grilling sausage with its mild, savoury flavour

The pork used to make the Brazilian sausage Linguiça comes from the topside, i.e. the ham, of the pig, which is why it is particularly well suited to smoking, frying and grilling. The lean meat is cut into coarse pieces and combined with spices such as paprika, oregano and garlic. It is typically always seasoned with “pimenta” and “sal” – pepper or chilli and salt. Sometimes cumin and cinnamon are added too, before the meat is left to rest. It can then be stuffed into the casing. One way of preparing **Linguiça brasileira** is to soak it in brine overnight. The brine makes the sausage’s flavour more pronounced, while it still remains mild. Very often the sausage is smoked, as this makes it keep longer.
Discover the variety of Brazilian cuisine with Linguiça Brasileira

Today, Brazilian cuisine is unthinkable without Linguiça Brasileira. Alongside carne-seca (dried meat), this Brazilian sausage is the most important ingredient in an original Brazilian Feijoada. Feijoada is a Brazilian bean stew with meat that gets its tasty smoky note from the addition of Linguiça. The sausage gets its typical mild, savoury flavour from the smoking process. That is why it is suited not only to soups, stews, pasta or sandwiches but also, perfectly, to our signature Churrasco, which you can enjoy at our steakhouse in an authentic Brazilian atmosphere. In Churrasco, the meat or sausage is marinated and then grilled on the skewer so that it stays tender and juicy. **That is why Linguiça and Churrasco go together “muito bem”, as Brazilians say – “perfectly”.**
A sausage inspired by Italy: Linguiça tipo Calabresa

Linguiça calabresa is a sausage similar to Salsiccia di Calabria, made by Italian immigrants from Calabria in the Bixiga district of São Paulo and seasoned with Calabrian chilli. The special seasoning with “pimenta calabresa” gave the sausage its characteristically spicy flavour and the name **Linguiça calabresa**. Today it is a popular type of sausage in Brazil and has been declared a sausage type in its own right by a law of the Brazilian Ministry of Agriculture. It is made exclusively from cured pork with the addition of Calabrian chilli and, where applicable, other spices that determine the sausage’s special flavour. It can be used for cooking or smoked. In Brazil, Linguiça calabresa is especially popular as the smoked sausage variety for topping pizza.
Discover Linguiça and carne on the skewer — a warm welcome awaits you

Try our **Churrasco Linguiça** or other grilled specialities from Brazil at our Churrascaria and discover the variety of Brazilian cuisine with us. We serve our Churrasco meat “na brasa”, which means “grilled over charcoal”. Choose from a range of juicy, tender meat skewers, or decide to taste the spicy **Brazilian grilling sausage** Linguiça, grilled on the skewer as Churrasco. Discover the taste of Brazil, the “sabor do Brasil”, and enjoy an evening of Brazilian flair at our restaurant. A warm welcome awaits you!

caipirinha.title: Original Caipirinha from Brazil – pure joie de vivre

blocks.text: What would a Brazilian meal be without Caipirinha, the country’s most famous cocktail? In Brazil, this popular drink is served on the beach, in the city, in every bar and in every restaurant. Its refreshing taste of lime, cachaça, sugar, ice cubes and a few other ingredients goes perfectly with Churrasco.

Relatively few ingredients are combined to make it, yet they create that incomparable taste which instantly brings to mind sunshine, summer flair and the Brazilian joy of life. Alongside other cocktails, long drinks and an exquisite selection of wines, you will find the **original Brazilian Caipirinha** on the menu at our steakhouse.
The magic cocktail ingredient: sugar cane

In Brazil, sugar cane was grown by slaves on the country’s large plantations, and the plant quickly became an important trade commodity for the inhabitants. As early as the 18th century, the enslaved workers liked to drink the sugar cane juice obtained from the plant. They prevented fermentation by boiling it, and so obtained a juice they called “garapa”. Sugar cane, cana de açúcar in Portuguese, originally comes from East Asia and reached the Middle East and Europe through trade. The Portuguese eventually brought the plant to South America with colonisation, and Brazil is still the world’s leading producer of sugar cane today. The juice obtained from it is processed further into a spirit, cachaça, which is the main element of the **Caipirinha**, often simply called “Caipi” in this part of the world. The name Caipirinha derives from the Brazilian word caipira, which translates as “country dweller”. Following the feminine form in Portuguese, German speakers say “die Caipirinha”; in Switzerland and Germany, however, “der Caipirinha” is also common. Originally a drink of the rural population, it is now known and appreciated worldwide.
Brazil’s most famous cocktail

To this day, the Caipirinha is listed among the Contemporary Classics of the International Bartenders Association, whose members include over 60 countries around the world. Various ways of preparing the Caipirinha cocktail are common, but there is only one original recipe by which the drink is typically made. Unlike in Europe, where brown cane sugar is widely used, Brazil uses only fine white cane sugar, which gives the drink its characteristic taste. Cane sugar in Europe is often coarse-grained and light brown in colour, which is why using brown sugar has become established here. A Brazilian, however, would never make an **authentic Caipirinha cocktail** with brown sugar, so as not to distort the taste. At our Churrascaria, we attach the greatest importance to a genuine Brazilian feel. That is why we serve the Caipirinha only in the original Brazilian version with white sugar. Using a pestle, the limes cut into quarters and the white sugar are pressed, then topped up with cachaça. It is important that the ends and core of the limes are always removed so that the cocktail does not taste too bitter. Cachaça has an alcohol content of at least 38%. Unlike rum, only pure sugar cane juice is used – no molasses or syrup.

A **genuine Caipirinha from Brazil** is topped up with ice cubes. The European version of the recipe uses crushed ice. Because Brazilians like to drink their Caipirinha ice-cold, even in the hot temperatures that prevail in Brazil, they prefer ice cubes for their cocktail. Ice in cube form keeps the glass and the drink cold for longer. Fresh lime, ice, white sugar and cachaça instantly evoke that typical feeling of warmth, sunshine and enjoyment, Brazilian style.
Boinabrasa signature drink – Caipirinha Maracuja

To give you an authentic experience at our steakhouse, **our Caipirinha cocktail is made solely to the original recipe.** We also offer our own fruity house version of this cult drink: the Caipirinha Maracuja. This cocktail, too, is made to the original Brazilian recipe, but with fresh passion fruit added instead of lime. The maracuja fruit is what defines our signature drink, because unlike many others we use no juice concentrate – only the pure juice of the fresh fruit, which we round off with a hint of syrup. Topped up with cachaça and ice, it gives you a particularly fruity version of the original Caipirinha with the incomparable aroma of fresh passion fruit. Spend your evening with us at the Churrascaria with excellent Brazilian skewers and a typical Caipirinha made to the original Brazilian recipe – classic or as the Caipirinha Maracuja variation. You can also order both cocktails without alcohol.
Experience Brazilian joie de vivre at our Churrascaria

Enjoy a **genuine Caipirinha do Brasil** with your Churrasco and other specialities at our restaurant, and experience the spirit of South America’s most beautiful country – we look forward to your visit. Whether you would like to have lunch or dinner with the finest Churrasco-style meat skewers on your own, with your family, with friends or with colleagues, set off on a culinary journey and complement your meal with a Caipirinha cocktail made to the original recipe. We will be glad to serve you in our cosy, authentic atmosphere. Immerse yourself in the incomparable taste of Brazil and discover the genuine Brazilian way of life.

gerichte.title: Brazilian dishes with fire and flavour

blocks.text: Today, in Brazil and its capital Brasilia, eating is far more than simply taking in food — rather, it is a celebration of coming together in a warm atmosphere. That is why **Brazilian dishes** are prepared with love, cooked for many people and served so that they are easy to share, so the country’s delicacies invite larger groups to enjoy them together.

**Brazilian cuisine** is wide-ranging, because European, Asian and African influences – through immigration from Europe, colonisation and slavery from Africa – have also shaped the only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas in culinary terms. Ingredients that could be cooked en masse and keep for a long time — such as nutritious cassava, rice and black beans — form the basis of Brazil’s dishes. Because of the blending of different cuisines, there is not really such a thing as **typical Brazilian food** in the classic sense. Cooking varies greatly from region to region.
The special features of Brazilian cuisine

But there are also dishes that have caught on nationwide. These include Brazil’s national dish, Feijoada (a hearty stew of pieces of meat with indispensable black beans, served with rice and toasted cassava flour on the side), which is said to taste best in Rio de Janeiro in particular.

South America’s largest country brings together various culinary influences, and besides the national dish Feijoada there are several other **typically Brazilian dishes** and drinks to discover:

Recreating the full variety of Brazilian cuisine 1:1 in our restaurant is practically an impossible task.
Instead, our appealing buffet of 25 different hot and cold dishes and side dishes is very extensive and offers a broad insight into the culinary influences that a wide range of regions have had on Brazilian cuisine – including German, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, African and indigenous dishes and delicacies. We use first-class, fresh products of the highest quality and offer you a selection of vegetarian and meat-free options.

**Brazilian dishes and specialities with meat** are famous — such as Churrasco. You can discover this popular Brazilian dish, authentically prepared, at our Churrascaria. Churrasco stands for the Brazilian art of grilling, in which the meat is seasoned to a Brazilian recipe in a carefully thought-out, step-by-step process, turned on the skewer and grilled – until the delicious meat speciality is served hot, crispy and juicy. Brazilian cuisine shows great finesse at the grill.
Brazilian specialities: meat the Churrasqueiros’ way

Although Churrasco comes from Brazil, it is eaten beyond the country’s borders, throughout Latin America as well as in Spain and Portugal. Depending on the region, there are subtle differences in ingredients, preparation and the way it is served. Unlike in Argentina, where only beef is used for Churrasco, in Brazil skilled Churrasqueiros prepare specialities from various kinds of meat:

The Churrasqueiros are professionally trained grill masters who work the fire skilfully and proudly with finely cut pieces of meat, following centuries of tradition just as their ancestors did: carefully skewered with the fatty side down and grilled evenly on all sides over an open fire, turning continuously. This keeps the meat crispy on the outside, tender on the inside and aromatically seasoned. The Passadores keep bringing fresh supplies of meat straight to the guests’ tables, where it is carved fresh from the skewer into appetising bite-sized pieces. This special way of serving meat is called Rodizio – “that which turns”.

Now you probably want to try Churrasco for yourself — you are welcome to visit our steakhouse for the experience. As for beef, we serve our guests the “Picanha” skewer of wonderfully tender beef rump from the Tafelspitz — authentically Brazilian, with the layer of fat left on the muscle.
Grilled delights at our Churrascaria

At our Churrascaria in Zurich-Dielsdorf, you can experience the high art of Brazilian Churrasco with up to 10 different varieties from the grill, right at your lavishly laid table – with your own eyes and your own palate. This traditional **Brazilian meat dish** is one of the absolute highlights of Brazil’s cuisine and combines wonderfully with the 25 hot and cold dishes on our buffet. You can rely on the highest quality and the best origin of our meat, which, depending on the type, we source from selected long-standing partners.

With a large plate of your own filled with Brazil’s colourful and varied cuisine, you will feel as if you were in Rio de Janeiro. This authentic ambience matters just as much to us in our own restaurant as attentive service and the high quality of our food.
Influences from around the world: colourful living, colourful cooking

But how do Brazil’s many cultures show in its cuisine? Chillies, plantains and coconut milk, for example, are ingredients from African cuisine that reappear in Brazilian dishes – for instance in the Brazilian speciality Moqueca, with fish, tomatoes, peppers, coriander and palm oil. Two typical variants have emerged: Moqueca Baiana with African dendê oil, and Moqueca Capixaba, for which olive oil is traditionally used – known in turn as one of the main ingredients of Italian cuisine.

Cassava, whose flour is also an ingredient of the national dish Feijoada, is of indigenous origin, as are the seafood and fish of Brazilian dishes. In São Paulo you will even be surprised by sushi — Japanese restaurants are more common here than anywhere else in the world outside Japan.

The Portuguese roots show in the hearty cuisine of Minas Gerais (cozinha mineira), where you will also find desserts made from sugar, milk and caramel, as well as delicious cakes and sweets with fruit and coconut.
Boinabrasa — typical Brazilian food

Family-run by Brazilian Swiss since 2013: our restaurant BOINABRASA offers the authentic cuisine and meat dishes of Brazil in the heart of Switzerland — save yourself the long journey to southern Brazil and try **Brazilian dishes** and drinks with us, on a menu that combines a selected “all-you-can-eat” buffet with fixed CHF prices. Of course, you can also raise a glass of the classic Brazilian cocktail, the Caipirinha — in style, with fresh lime, cachaça, white sugar and ice. But you can also order alcohol-free cocktails, beer and wine, as well as tropical fruit juices with mango and maracuja. Do you have questions about typical Brazilian food? We will be happy to advise you on which drink goes with which dish and, if you wish, introduce you to the house recommendations.

Anyone interested in a “**gaucho grill**” is looking for a culinary journey through South America that ends with meat that is crispy on the outside and wonderfully juicy on the inside, prepared using the traditional South American art of grilling. Anyone who says “gaucho grill”, however, is using a rather misleading term and usually means beef prepared the Argentinian way. Less often, the term is used for Brazilian Churrasco – the Brazilian way of preparing meat that we celebrate at our Churrascaria Boinabrasa.

The problem is the misconception that the term “gaucho” applies to just one group of people – Argentinians – and is primarily associated with the famous Argentinian beef steaks. Some people also use the term when looking for a grill on which meat can be cooked perfectly in South American style.

At this point we would like to clear up a few misunderstandings – simply because there is no one gaucho grill – and take you on a little culinary journey through South America.
Meaning: not all gauchos are the same

In German-speaking countries, the term “Gauchos” is mostly used as a general term for Argentinians. In football, for example, it is quite common to call the Argentinian team the “Gauchos” – even though in recent years the term has increasingly been seen as disparaging and generalising. The thing is: the gauchos, historically the descendants of Iberian immigrants, were and are found throughout South America. Not only in Argentina but also in Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Bolivia, the gauchos were known as cattle breeders on the pampas; their most important products included dried meat and cowhide – and depending on where they lived, they developed particular culinary and cultural rituals and customs. Today, the gauchos’ descendants mostly live in rural settlements and don’t have much to do with modern urban society. Their influence, however, can be felt almost everywhere in South America – and tasted!
The gaucho art of grilling in Argentina

Argentinian gauchos love their beef. They are famous for it around the world; it is an export hit and deeply woven into the country’s culture. For many Argentinians, the gauchos are simply folk heroes who shaped the country’s identity.

Thanks to the gauchos, Argentinians have their very own idea of grilling. They use the term “Asado” for a grilling method in which large pieces of meat – or often whole animals, skin and head included – are set up around a fire in a cross shape on so-called metal asado crosses and cooked there for hours. Alongside this, the grill master, the “Asador”, usually runs a parrilla, a charcoal grill with a grate on which smaller pieces of meat are cooked too. Both set-ups are sometimes called a “**gaucho grill**” internationally, which is simply imprecise.

By Argentinian custom, the meat is served without sauces or marinades and at most lightly salted, so that the authentic flavour of the meat takes centre stage. This method dates back to the days when the gaucho cattle breeders would still slaughter whole animals and cook them for hours over a campfire. Today, an authentic asado is a cultural event celebrated with family and friends. The fires often reach an impressive size and draw people from the surrounding area to join the celebration.
Is there a Brazilian “gaucho grill”?

In the 19th century, the Brazilian gauchos invented a very special way of preparing meat over an open flame – Churrasco – and celebrated it in grand style at public festivals and family celebrations, birthdays and weddings. Today, Churrascarias, i.e. Churrasco restaurants, can be found all over Brazil, and it is still customary to gather family and friends there for a meal. Meats of various origins are prepared, from beef steak to pork neck and spare ribs to poultry. Churrascarias now inspire grill masters all over the world – for example our restaurant Boinabrasa in Zurich. We don’t just offer authentic meat prepared in the Brazilian Churrasco style. We want to offer our guests the same convivial atmosphere that Brazilians value so highly.

A Brazilian grill master would never say “gaucho grill” – because just as diverse as the gauchos were, and as widely as they spread across South America, so differently did their grill masters’ habits develop. That is why a clear distinction must be made between, for example, Brazilian Churrasco and the Argentinian “gaucho grill”.

By the way: strictly speaking, Churrasco also exists in Brazil, but the word is used differently. Argentinians usually use the term only for a thick-cut beef steak, mostly the ribeye with its high fat content. For Argentinians, a skewer of chicken thighs or pork neck, for example, is not Churrasco – unlike for Brazilians, who call any meat cooked on a churrasqueira (a Churrasco grill) Churrasco. Incidentally, the same focus on beef can also be found in Paraguay and Uruguay.
Confusing terminology? Drop the term!

So anyone who uses the term “**gaucho grill**” can very easily be misunderstood. It is better to use terms such as “Brazilian Churrasco” or “Argentinian asado” – otherwise you will have to put up with people asking which “gauchos” exactly you actually mean. Between ourselves, it is even best to avoid the term “gaucho” altogether when it comes to food, because it is too generalising and undermines the cultural and culinary diversity of South America.
Is Boinabrasa a “gaucho grill” restaurant?

No – we are a Churrascaria run on the Brazilian model. Besides, hardly any South American-inspired restaurant would call itself a “gaucho grill”. The term was dreamt up mainly by American marketers of charcoal grills and has somehow caught on in German-speaking countries too. If South Americans stood outside our door and read “gaucho grill”, they would rightly scratch their heads and ask: which gauchos? Argentinian or Brazilian – or perhaps even Paraguayan or Uruguayan? Likewise, our German-speaking guests would assume we run an Argentinian steakhouse – because most people associate the term gaucho with Argentinians. No: we are a Churrasco restaurant on the Brazilian model!

If you want to try the famous meat prepared in the Brazilian Churrasco style, you don’t necessarily have to travel far. We look forward to taking you on this culinary journey!
